claims.claim: Consumer buying behavior refers to the decisions and actions people undertake to buy products or services for personal use; consumers make buying decisions nearly every day and give most of them little thought.
The consumer market is made up of all the individuals and households who buy goods and services for personal use.

Buying behavior is not influenced solely by the external environment; it is also determined by the buyer's level of involvement in the purchase and the amount of risk involved — habitual buying behavior is a low-involvement repeat buy with little perceived brand difference, while complex buying behavior occurs for significant or expensive purchases that involve research.

Cultural factors comprise a set of values or ideologies of a particular community or group of individuals; culture refers to the values, ideas, and attitudes that are learned and shared among members of a group, and cultural factors can include culture, subcultures, social class, and gender.
Social factors — the influences of family, reference groups, roles and status — have a huge impact on buying behavior; reference groups include opinion leaders, people who influence others.
Personal factors such as occupation, age and life-cycle stage, economic situation, lifestyle, and personality and self-concept play a major role in buying behavior.
Psychological factors that influence buying behavior include motivation, perception, learning, beliefs, and attitudes.

A buyer passes through five stages of the consumer decision process: need recognition (sensing a difference between the actual state and the desired state), information search (which can include asking friends and family for opinions), evaluation of alternatives (viewing a product as a bundle of attributes), purchase decision (often using heuristics — mental shortcuts such as price-equals-quality and brand loyalty), and post-purchase evaluation (satisfaction is a function of the closeness between the buyer's expectations and the product's perceived performance; doubts after purchase lead to cognitive dissonance, or buyer's remorse).

All purchase behavior is in some sense ethical, involving moral judgment; economic theory's picture of consumers seeking to maximize utility at the lowest cost is a theoretical model, and real buying behavior includes shortcuts, habit, and second-guessing.
Marketing involves gaining a better understanding of the customer's interests, tastes, and preferences — the serve-the-customer purpose that frames why marketers study consumer behavior.
Consumer behavior is a recognized core field of marketing study; the American Marketing Association maintains a topic library on consumer behavior.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many stages are in the consumer decision process?
positions: OpenStax's Principles of Marketing describes five stages: need recognition, information search, evaluation of alternatives, purchase decision, and post-purchase evaluation.
Some textbooks compress or extend the process (e.g., adding a separate post-purchase behavior stage or merging search and evaluation).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: This lesson teaches the five-stage model exactly as OpenStax names it, and notes that the process is a model rather than a strict checklist — habitual purchases skip or shorten stages.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Are there four factor groups or five?
positions: The classic framework names four groups of factors: cultural, social, personal, and psychological.
OpenStax's learning outcomes for section 3.2 list situational factors as a fifth category alongside the four.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the classic four as the core framework (as required by the topic brief), and mentions in one clause that some treatments add situational factors.

positions: Economic theory has modeled consumers as utility maximizers who seek the most satisfaction at the lowest cost.
OpenStax's treatment of the decision process shows buyers using heuristics (mental shortcuts), buying on habit, and experiencing cognitive dissonance or buyer's remorse.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson includes an honest note: buyers are not perfectly rational — shortcuts, habits, and second-guessing are documented parts of real buying behavior.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Marketing, Section 3.1: Understanding Consumer Markets and Buying Behavior
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A backbone. openstax.org blocks direct fetches; verified via an Internet Archive capture dated 2023-02-04. Supports: the working definition of consumer buying behavior as the decisions and actions people undertake to buy products or services for personal use; the consumer market as all individuals and households buying for personal use; the observation that consumers make buying decisions nearly every day and give most of them little thought; the buyer's black box (stimulus-response) model; and types of buying behavior including habitual buying behavior (low involvement, repeat buy, little perceived brand difference) and complex buying behavior (significant or expensive purchases with research). Concepts adapted into original prose; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Marketing, Section 3.2: Factors That Influence Consumer Buying Behavior
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A backbone. Verified via an Internet Archive capture dated 2023-02-03. Supports: the four classic factor groups — cultural factors (a set of values or ideologies of a community; culture as values, ideas, and attitudes learned and shared among members of a group), social factors (family, reference groups, roles and status; opinion leaders as people who influence others), personal factors (occupation, age and life-cycle stage, economic situation, lifestyle, personality and self-concept), and psychological factors (motivation, perception, learning, beliefs, attitudes). The book's learning outcomes also list situational factors as a fifth category; the lesson teaches the classic four as its core. Psychological depth is owned by the psychology subject and referenced only. Concepts adapted into original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Marketing, Section 3.3: The Consumer Purchasing Decision Process
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A backbone. Verified via an Internet Archive capture dated 2023-02-03. Supports: the five-stage consumer decision process — Stage 1 need recognition (sensing a difference between the actual and desired state), Stage 2 information search (internal, external, and experiential search, including asking friends and family for opinions), Stage 3 evaluation of alternatives (products as bundles of attributes), Stage 4 purchase decision (including heuristics such as price-equals-quality and brand loyalty), Stage 5 post-purchase evaluation (satisfaction as the closeness between expectations and perceived performance; cognitive dissonance, or buyer's remorse). Concepts adapted into original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Marketing, Section 3.4: Ethical Issues in Consumer Buying Behavior
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A backbone. Verified via an Internet Archive capture dated 2023-02-04. Supports: all purchase behavior is in some sense ethical, involving moral judgment (consumers weighing human-rights and animal-welfare concerns in purchases); ethical consumerism; and economic theory's utility-maximizing consumer as a theoretical model rather than a full description of real behavior. Used to ground the honest note (buyers are not perfectly rational) and the ethical framing of the lesson. Concepts adapted into original prose.
